known_from_text.basis: Verses 2–3 request a hearing; verse 10 describes daily calling and outstretched hands; verse 14 renews the appeal in the morning.
known_from_text.claim: The speaker continues addressing God throughout severe distress.

known_from_text.basis: Verses 4–7 invoke Sheol, the pit, the dead, and the grave; verses 9 and 19 describe companions being removed.
known_from_text.claim: The lament portrays suffering as proximity to death and exclusion from ordinary companionship.

known_from_text.basis: Direct second-person statements in verses 7–9 and 19 describe God placing, afflicting, and removing companions; verses 17–18 describe God’s wrath and terrors.
known_from_text.claim: The speaker explicitly attributes the affliction and separation to God.

known_from_text.basis: Verse 11 asks about wonders and the shades rising to give thanks; verses 12–13 ask whether divine loyalty, faithfulness, wonders, and righteousness are recounted or known.
known_from_text.claim: The Hebrew questions connect death with the problem of praising and making God’s deeds known.

known_from_text.basis: Verses 11–13 use “reach me,” “find me,” and “when I’ve been forgotten” where the Hebrew asks about doing wonders, recounting, and knowing.
known_from_text.claim: The setting changes those questions toward personal accessibility to God’s care.

known_from_text.basis: Verses 17–19 remain within wrath, encirclement, removed companions, and darkness.
known_from_text.claim: The psalm ends without a narrated rescue or divine reply.

not_known_from_text.claim: Heman personally composed the psalm or experienced every circumstance described.
not_known_from_text.why_not: The heading supplies an association; it does not independently establish authorship or an autobiographical identity for the speaker.

not_known_from_text.claim: The speaker has a particular illness, psychiatric diagnosis, or literal imprisonment.
not_known_from_text.why_not: Pain, failing eyes, confinement, and proximity to death describe distress without identifying its medical or historical cause.

not_known_from_text.claim: The suffering is punishment for a specified wrongdoing.
not_known_from_text.why_not: The lament names divine wrath but provides no particular offense or explanatory judgment.

not_known_from_text.claim: The questions establish a comprehensive doctrine denying resurrection or any existence after death.
not_known_from_text.why_not: They function as urgent questions within a lament; they do not present a systematic account of the afterlife.

not_known_from_text.claim: The speaker is eventually rescued or permanently abandoned.
not_known_from_text.why_not: The poem supplies neither a subsequent outcome nor a statement covering all future time.

not_known_from_text.claim: Selah specifies an exact pause, instrumental interlude, or duration.
not_known_from_text.why_not: The markers are present, but the supplied text does not define their performance.

guardrails.cultic_setting: The song designation, director’s instruction, and Korahite association support a musical worship setting. Direct address to YHWH, prayer, outstretched palms, and concern for praise reinforce that setting. The text does not specify a temple location, particular rite, festival, sacrifice, instrument, or division of singers; the technical heading terms do not securely supply a recoverable tune or performance procedure.
guardrails.heading_attribution: The Hebrew heading identifies a song and psalm, associates it with the sons of Korah, addresses the director, includes the direction Mahalath Leannoth, and identifies a maskil associated with Heman the Ezrahite. These are received attributions and performance indications. They do not independently establish personal authorship, identify the first-person speaker as Heman, or document a historical occasion. The English omits the heading.

analyses.method: Compared the supplied English with the supplied Masoretic Hebrew, token glosses, and immediate context. Literal backbones in the verse audits served as compact checks of agency, actions, images, and relationships, not proposed replacement lyrics. No external edition or lexicon was consulted. Section titles here are analytical descriptions: the verse-aligned setting supplies no section labels. The sections cover all nineteen Masoretic verses, including the untranslated heading; Selah alignment is measured against those sections. No separate performance apparatus appears in this setting.

analyses.summary: The setting retains the psalm’s movement from urgent prayer through proximity to death, divine wrath, isolation, questions about the dead, renewed prayer, and a final return to darkness. Its short lines and conversational expressions make the lament immediate and personal. The largest shift occurs in verses 11–13: questions about wonders, praise, and the recognition of God’s faithfulness among the dead become questions about whether God can reach the speaker. Elsewhere, images of breaking and being undone soften explicit dying and destruction into personal disintegration. The ending preserves the absence of a reported answer or deliverance, while “my closest friend” intensifies an interpretive personification of darkness.

omissions.rationale: The setting does not render the superscription.
The causal connector introducing the speaker’s troubles is absent.
The destination of those going down, the pit, is absent from this verse’s rendering.
Being set free or released among the dead receives no distinct rendering.
The grave image does not explicitly identify its occupants as slain.
The reference to all the breakers is reduced to waves without the comprehensive modifier.
Neither Selah appears in the setting.

The question about reaching the speaker does not carry the explicit reference to wonders.
The question about retaining a voice omits the shades arising.
The question about hiding God’s face leaves “from me” unexpressed.
